claims.text: An optimal intermediate concentration of surface nitrogen vacancies in Mo2N enhances dehydrogenation selectivity relative to both low- and excessively high-vacancy Mo2N.
Standard nitridation conditions produce Mo2N with minimal nitrogen-vacancy concentrations.
Changing nitridation temperature and ammonia flow rate can systematically vary the surface nitrogen-vacancy density of Mo2N.
Surface and morphological characterization can help distinguish vacancy effects from coincident structural changes.
Surface nitrogen vacancies in Mo2N serve as catalytically active sites for dehydrogenation.
Nitrogen vacancies alter the adsorption geometry of dehydrogenation reactants on Mo2N.
Nitrogen vacancies alter reactant binding energies on Mo2N.
Adsorbate binding strength can govern intermediate stability and activation barriers in transition-metal catalysis.
An optimal vacancy density favors the preferred dehydrogenation pathway and thereby increases target-product selectivity.
Changes in the structure or nuclearity of catalytic sites can reverse or substantially alter product selectivity.
Intermediate-vacancy Mo2N will have higher target-product selectivity than dense, low-vacancy Mo2N under otherwise identical dehydrogenation conditions.
The proposed vacancy-selectivity relationship is expected to hold in a flow reactor at 300–400 °C with controlled gas composition and flow rate.
The same vacancy-selectivity relationship may not hold outside 300–400 °C.
Morphological changes caused by catalyst synthesis may be intertwined with changes in nitrogen-vacancy density and catalytic selectivity.
XPS can be used to quantify nitrogen-vacancy density in the proposed Mo2N catalyst series.
An absence of a significant relationship between measured vacancy density and dehydrogenation selectivity would falsify the hypothesis.
